https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/02/two-die-.text: Two firefighting helicopters collided in Greece on Sunday while helping control a huge wildfire northwest of Athens that has destroyed more than 100 homes, as people fled another blaze on the tourist island of Kefalonia. Two people on one helicopter — a Greek and a Danish national — died, while the crew on the other, one person from Greece, one from Britain, survived, the fire service said. Investigations had started into what caused the collision, it added. Europe has been ravaged by wildfires this summer after a period of record-breaking heatwaves and little rain – conditions that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. Destructive blazes in France and Spain showed some signs of easing over the weekend, but several wildfires have broken out in Greece after a period of relative calm there. The two helicopters collided in the area of Psatha in the Attica region, Greece's fire service said in a statement. Video posted on the Forecast Weather Greece Facebook page appeared to show two helicopters closing to cross paths at low altitude, before the main rotor of the lower helicopter struck the underside of the other. The lower one then crashed in flames. The second helicopter then dumped its load of water and flew away. Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the footage. Investigations suggested the fire that started in the Greek region of Boeotia before spreading to Attica was caused by sparks from conductors on a private network transmitting electricity generated by wind turbines to the main power grid, the eKathimerini website reported. Two Greek nationals were arrested on suspicion of negligence, while another suspect remains at large, the report said. 'Force of nature' Gale-force winds that had fuelled a fire around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth 60 km (40 miles) northwest of Athens subsided, but flames crossed a mountain to the south and reached the settlement of Veniza and a military firing range, igniting unexploded ordnance. Emergency crews focused their efforts on preventing fire from advancing towards the coastal town of Megara, which has a population of around 30,000. "There are moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions exceed all human planning and every operational capability," Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in his regular Sunday message. Greek authorities issued emergency evacuation alerts for a number of settlements in western Attica, including an industrial estate near Megara. In the village of Agios Konstantinos, residents were doing their best to halt the spread of the blaze. "The fire has been burning since last night, it is certain that they cannot have forces everywhere. We as residents are doing everything we can," said Tasos Tzempelikos, 61, who along with his son was pouring water on the fire. Overnight, several settlements on the Ionian island of Kefalonia were evacuated after a fire broke out in the Pastra area in the south. Fire in France changes course In France, a fire in the southwestern Var region switched direction after a change in the wind and surged into a forested area that was difficult to access, BFM TV reported. A new fire also broke out alongside a highway near the historic southern city of Carcassonne, apparently caused by a blazing vehicle, BFM TV added. Video on the channel showed huge plumes of billowing grey smoke and flames near the road. Authorities said they had closed the highway and evacuated a nearby animal park. In Montfort-sur-Argens in Var, Georges Blanc, who had fled the fire earlier, returned home and was busy putting out hot embers to prevent a flare-up, while firefighters watered the wider area. "With the combined efforts of the two Canadairs (firefighting planes) and the firefighters, I think you could say all the houses were saved ... And now, well, I'm coming back to check, because since I saw the flames, I thought the houses wouldn't have survived," he told Reuters. In central Spain, wildfires that ripped through tens of thousands of hectares over the past week were mostly under control, though firefighters were dealing with reignitions in some areas. In the western province of Caceres, a forest blaze erupted on Saturday, prompting the evacuation of around 800 people. Those residents were allowed to return on Sunday but remained confined to their homes as the fire was still active. Hungary nuclear plant forced to shut Other European countries are struggling with drought and receding water levels in major rivers, including the Rhine and the Danube, which recorded its lowest-ever water levels in Hungary, Serbia and Romania. Hungary faces a critical five days, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, as the drying out of the Danube forced the country's sole nuclear power plant to shut for the first time in more than four decades, with a new heatwave looming. Falls in water levels amid a lack of rain have also disrupted shipping and tourism in Hungary and triggered water-use restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. Danube levels in Serbia fell to their lowest since 1985, cutting the daily output of the country's biggest hydropower plant to only 20%, the energy minister said on Sunday.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: When adding announced and pre-construction projects, the US is building nearly three times as much as its fellow global economic powerhouse. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen When adding announced and pre-construction projects, the US is building nearly three times as much as its fellow global economic powerhouse. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images US news US building twice as much gas-fired capacity as China in AI boom, analysis finds There has been a 76% increase in under-construction gas-fired projects amid ‘frenzy’ to build more datacenters Oliver Milman Tue 25 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 06.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US has surged ahead of China in the building of new gas-fired power generation, largely to feed a boom in artificial intelligence (AI) that is adding vast amounts of planet-heating emissions, a new analysis has found. For decades, China’s rapid economic growth has seen it outpace the US in the addition of new gas power generation but a recent “frenzy” in datacenter construction for AI has reversed this, said Global Energy Monitor (Gem) in its new report. The US is now building twice as much gas-fired capacity as China, and more than any other country in the world, after a stunning 76% increase in under-construction projects in the first half of this year. When adding announced and pre-construction projects, the US is building nearly three times as much as its fellow global economic powerhouse. Since January, gas power capacity in overall development in the US has ballooned by 50%, rising from 252GW to 378GW – a third of the global total. If all of these projects are ultimately built, the US will increase its gas fleet by around two-thirds at a capital cost of more than $647bn, Gem found. Bar chart showing the US’s in development gas power capacity tripling China’s Around half of the new capacity is directly tied to a rash of upcoming datacenters that require a huge amount of electricity to handle the increased demand from AI. Using gas, a fossil fuel that is dangerously overheating our planet, rather than renewables to power this glut of new datacenters threatens to increase US power emissions by as much as 20%, according to one estimate . “Six months ago, China had more gas plants under construction but that has now flipped,” said Jenny Martos, a project manager at Global Energy Monitor. “There has been an enormous surge in datacenter proposals powered by gas in the past year and the climate implications of that is huge. Building all of this gas for AI locks in decades of pollution and it is also locking in dependence on a volatile fuel cost, which will get passed down to rate payers.” Donald Trump and others in his administration have repeatedly claimed that China, the world’s largest carbon polluter, is expanding its fossil fuel use so much that any emissions cuts by the US would be futile. The president has said of China that “their air is dirty, and it drifts over to us”. But the rush of new infrastructure for AI, along with the Trump administration’s demolition of environmental regulations and China’s rapid adoption of clean energy, is changing this equation. US spending on power plants fueled by coal and gas will outstrip that of China for the first time in decades, the International Energy Agency has forecast . The stampede by tech companies, such as Google, Open AI and Amazon, to build datacenters has contributed to a backlog of the most efficient gas turbines used for accompanying power plants. This has led several companies, including Elon Musk’s xAI , to quickly switch to smaller, less efficient turbines which are more heavily polluting. Concerns over the climate crisis , rising power bills, tax breaks for AI companies and water shortages – two-thirds of more than 800 planned datacenters are located in drought-stricken areas – has fueled mounting local opposition to data center construction. A recent poll by Heatmap found that three-quarters of Americans do not want to live next to a datacenter, a huge increase in opposition in the past year. Dozens of cities and counties have placed restrictions on new datacenters, with New York in July becoming the first state to enact a temporary ban on new hyper-scale datacenter permitting and construction. Despite this backlash, which could well hurt Republicans in the November midterm elections, the Trump administration has championed the building of new datacenters and eliminated environmental reviews in order to speed them up. Trump said this month that “data centers could be bigger than oil” and state governors should cut taxes to encourage them. “Frankly, communities that don’t take a datacenter, they’re making a mistake because there’s plenty of communities that want them,” Trump said in separate remarks to his former lawyer Michael Cohen last week. “Because it means jobs, and it means tremendous tax revenue coming into the towns and cities that take them.” Explore more on these topics US news Fossil fuels China Gas Energy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

Photograph: Jigme Dorje/Xinhua/AP Nepal-Tibet flood disaster China is concealing scale of flood disaster, say Tibet campaigners Rights group claims 300 homes were destroyed in Tibet and number of missing people is ‘far higher’ than Beijing admits Danny Vincent in Hong Kong Mon 31 Aug 2026 05.18 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 05.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Tibetan advocacy group says hundreds of homes were destroyed on the Tibetan side of the border in last week’s deadly floods, raising questions about Beijing’s official account of the scale of the disaster. Public discussion about the flash floods has been restricted, with security officials in Tibet announcing on Sunday that it had penalised at least 10 people for sharing “false disaster information”. There was no further information on the nature of the penalties. Chinese authorities say 16 people have been confirmed dead and 546 are missing, including 261 foreign citizens. But the International Campaign for Tibet says its sources believe the number of casualties is significantly higher, with at least 300 homes destroyed. Tencho Gyatso, the president of the campaign group, told the Guardian: “What is visible in Nepal exposes what is being concealed in Tibet. Four villages – Sale, Serchung, Labi and Rizi – were among the hardest hit, with approximately 300 homes reportedly destroyed and many people still missing.” She said the “little information that we can gather from the ground” suggested the numbers affected were “far higher” than Chinese officials had reported. On 26 August, the collapse of a glacier triggered deadly floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, destroying entire villages. The death toll on the Nepal side has passed 900, with more than 4,000 missing. Tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada among others remain unaccounted for in the mountainous region that is popular with trekkers and pilgrims. Advocacy groups say there has been a stark contrast in the amount of information presented on either side of the border. Chinese coverage has been dominated by official state media reports, with few unofficial accounts about the scale of the disaster and its aftermath. View image in fullscreen Nepali soldiers retrieve bodies of people swept away by the flash floods and a mudslide on the Narayani River. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters Independent verification is extremely difficult in Tibet, where foreign journalists face severe restrictions. Tibetans can face imprisonment for sharing information with journalists and advocacy groups outside China . Gyatso said: “Officially released glimpses, however important, cannot tell us what is happening across all affected communities.” Her Tibetan advocacy group said several sources reported that survivors had been moved to Gyirong, which is about 30km (18 miles) from the border crossing that was hit by the flooding. They are said to be under strict management and restricted from communicating freely. According to a report posted on 27 August on the Tibet Daily, a state-run newspaper, two Tibetans were detained for questioning for posting “rumours” that more than 1,000 people had been swept away close to the border. Map showing the area of the disaster Gyatso said: “The Chinese government portrays it like it’s only happening in Nepal and there’s nothing across the border. For any type of crisis, the way China handles it is that there is no crisis. The party is in control.” Posts relating to the disaster continued to trend on Chinese social media on Monday, with many comments echoing official narratives and supporting rescue efforts. A Weibo post by Hu Xijin – a prominent Chinese commentator and former chief editor of the state-run Global Times – attracted more than 300 comments and thousands of likes. He accused a small number of voices of seeking to “stir controversy by fabricating baseless claims”. However, one comment under his post questioned why all the updates were coming from the Nepali side of the border. View image in fullscreen Rescuers use sniffer dogs to search for mudslide victims in Gyirong in Tibet. Photograph: Jigme Dorje/Xinhua/AP On Sunday, Tibetan public security officials said they had penalised people for sharing misleading information or “disrupting online order” with posts about the disaster. In one case, a user identified only as Zhang disputed the official death toll, posting: “Clearly thousands of people were swept away, yet the authorities reported only three deaths and 265 people missing.” How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Read more Another user named Zhou said: “In this wave of mudslides, one entire village was wiped out. It was definitely more than a thousand [deaths].” Maya Wang of Human Rights Watch said: “The instinct of the Chinese government is always to kind of control and to ensure the narrative which is to portray itself as a very efficient government. “There have been questions raised over how the development of the valleys in an ecologically fragile and geologically fragile area may have related to this disaster.” Human rights groups say that Beijing maintains tight controls over movement, religion and information in Tibet. Tibetan groups in exile have long been critical of large-scale development in the region, which they consider geologically fragile. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said ⁠on Monday that the ⁠release of ⁠information about the floods and mudslide near its ⁠border with Nepal was transparent and timely. “Malicious smear campaigns ‌and hype using the disaster situation does not align with popular sentiment,” said Guo Jiakun, ‌in response to allegations that China censored videos of the disaster and understated the number of missing people. When asked about allegations ‌that China ignored warnings from scientists over hydropower construction, he said: “We ⁠firmly oppose such baseless and malicious speculation.” Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei Explore more on these topics Nepal-Tibet flood disaster China Nepal Tibet Natural disasters Asia Pacific South and central Asia news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Nepal-Tibet floods: rescuers race to reach 900 people believed trapped in hydropower tunnels ‘The house got carried 100 metres away’: some Nepal flood victims had minutes of notice. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Indonesia kept several airports closed and shifted schools to remote learning on Monday as volcanic ash coated parts of Java and Sumatra. The eruption has halted about 2,300 flights and affected more than 268,000 passengers. Authorities say the volcano remains active with intermittent eruptions and ash emissions. The Geological Agency said the 25-hour eruption ended on Sunday but warned that more activity is likely in the coming days. Volcanic ash in the airspace around Jakarta and other cities prompted the closure of eight airports. Schools in affected areas moved to online learning to reduce exposure. Indonesia sits on the Pacific 'Ring of Fire' and has more than 120 active volcanoes. Egyptian journalists say the arrests are part of mounting pressure against the media. Photograph: AP View image in fullscreen Journalists with a symbolic coffin representing press freedom at a 2016 protest. Egyptian journalists say the arrests are part of mounting pressure against the media. Photograph: AP Global development Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood Supported by About this content Saher Ahmed in Cairo Fri 9 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 00.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention. Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood . The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers. One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny. “We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee. In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”. Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post. Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Journalists’ Syndicate, whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families. Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained Read more Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”. The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”. For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession. “We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.” Explore more on these topics Global development Press freedom Protest Newspapers & magazines Egypt Muslim Brotherhood Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
